title: {{NAME}} and the Princess of the Iron Palace
moral: The greatest kingdoms are built not on power, but on the willingness to ask for help.

pages.content:
The Iron Palace stood at the edge of the world like a challenge someone had forgotten to finish. Its towers were all pistons and gears, its battlements rows of quietly rotating cogs, and its gates were two enormous arms of polished copper that opened with the deep, satisfying sound of a well-made clock.

{{NAME}} had arrived by hot-air balloon, which had lost altitude over the mechanical kingdom and deposited him rather suddenly in the palace courtyard. The courtyard was full of robots, every shape and size imaginable, going about their business with quiet, efficient purpose.

The largest one, a butler-robot seven feet tall with a chest like a wardrobe, had swept {{NAME}} inside before he could say a word. "Her Highness is expecting someone," it announced, in a voice like a cello playing two notes at once. "You'll do."

The grand hall within smelled of warm metal and something floral, rose oil and steel, an odd combination that somehow worked entirely.

pages.content:
Princess Verity was not what {{NAME}} had expected, though he realised afterwards he wasn't sure what he had expected. She was perhaps a year older than him, with sharp dark eyes and a crown made entirely of small working gears that rotated slowly around her head, each one catching the light differently.

She was standing at an enormous drafting table covered in blueprints, and she turned to face {{NAME}} with the direct gaze of someone who had neither the time nor the patience for anything other than useful people.

"My chief engineer, Copperbolt, has frozen," she announced, gesturing at a tall, motionless robot in the corner with a faintly apologetic expression. "His memory drive has become too full. He needs it cleared, but only a person with no mechanical access codes can do it, because it requires a full manual reset from the outside panel." She looked at {{NAME}}'s hands. "Can you follow precise instructions?"

{{NAME}} had once rebuilt a bicycle from parts. He was reasonably confident.

pages.content:
Copperbolt's access panel was on his back, between his shoulder blades, a small brass door with nine micro-buttons in a specific sequence that Princess Verity recited from memory while {{NAME}} worked.

It was slow, fiddly, exacting work. The buttons were no bigger than apple seeds, and the sequence had forty-three steps. Verity read each one clearly, pausing when {{NAME}} needed extra time. She didn't rush him. She didn't hover. She simply stood beside him, steady as a lighthouse.

Three times {{NAME}}'s hand slipped. Three times Verity said, "Reset to step thirty-one," without a trace of impatience.

On the fourth attempt, button forty-three clicked home with a sound like a tiny chime. Copperbolt's chest-panel lit in a warm amber sequence. His head turned, slowly first, then smoothly. His eyes, two round circles of blue glass, blinked once, then focused on {{NAME}} with an expression of dignified gratitude.

"Rebooting complete," he announced, in a voice like a contented foghorn. "Systems clear. All functions restored."

Princess Verity exhaled a long, slow breath and gave a single, precise nod.

pages.content:
But as Copperbolt restarted, his first act was to run a palace-wide diagnostic, and what the diagnostic found was worse than a frozen engineer.

The palace's central power crystal, housed deep in the basement, was cracked. If it shattered, every robot in the Iron Palace would shut down simultaneously, and the kingdom's mechanical infrastructure would fail. The crack had been growing for weeks, but Copperbolt's frozen state had prevented him from flagging the alert.

They had, he informed them, twenty-two minutes.

"The crystal can be stabilised with copper-thread binding," Verity said, already moving, pulling coils of thin copper wire from a wall cabinet. "But it requires two people working simultaneously from opposite sides."

They ran the entire length of the palace, down three spiral staircases, through a room full of sleeping clockwork animals, and into the crystal chamber. The power crystal was cracked in a jagged line from top to bottom, pulsing a weak, irregular red.

On opposite sides of it, {{NAME}} and Verity began to wind. Their hands moved in mirror image, copper thread wrapping tighter and tighter, each loop stabilising the crack a fraction more.

pages.content:
The crystal blazed from red to amber to a deep, settled gold as the final loop of copper thread locked in place. The pulsing stopped. The palace hummed, low and even and content, like a cat who has found the best spot in the house.

Copperbolt appeared in the doorway and regarded them both with the expression of a being who had just experienced enormous relief and was managing it with considerable dignity. "Structural integrity restored," he said. "Your Highness. Young visitor."

Princess Verity looked at {{NAME}} across the now-glowing crystal. She reached up and removed one small gear from the edge of her crown and held it out to him. It was warm in his hand.

"For precise work under pressure," she said simply.

The balloon, it turned out, had drifted back to just outside the copper gates. {{NAME}} climbed in and rose gently into the golden sky, the gear in his pocket ticking very quietly against his fingertip. He was home before dark, warm and drowsy, the gear on the pillow beside him.

He fell asleep wondering what blueprints Verity had spread on that enormous table, and whether they were for something that had never been built before.
